channel_name: Invest Like the Best · Patrick O'Shaughnessy
video_title: What Happens When the AI Boom Runs Out of Money
gist: Ben Thompson argues the nearest-term AI constraint is not compute or power but money: the sector has burned through free cash flow and debt into equity issuance and vendor-financed deals, risking an 'air gap' before AI revenue can fund the buildout, even as AI itself keeps improving. He reframes intelligence and compute as commodities, sees TSMC/memory/Nvidia repeating the geopolitical and capital mistakes of past cycles, and handicaps Big Tech and frontier labs on whether their business models can survive a world where AI is abundant and marginal-cost pricing rules.

themes.theme: The AI Capital Gap and Funding Air Gap

insights.claim: The nearest-term binding constraint on the AI buildout may be capital, not compute or electricity, because AI capex is descending the capital curve from free cash flow to debt to equity issuance to vendor-financed vehicles, with no obvious funding source after that.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Watch the funding stack, not just GPU/power headlines; the tell of stress is escalating creativity in financing (equity raises, SPV-style structures) rather than free cash flow funding.
insights.quote: the nearest term question is are we going to have enough money which is kind of a bizarre thing to think about like that's what happened in in the 1870s like we the world just ran out of money

insights.claim: Even if AI capital funding blows up in an 'air gap' before revenue catches up, the underlying AI capability and its economic impact do not disappear, mirroring how railroads kept operating and contributing to GDP after the 1870s money ran out.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: A financing bust would be a buying opportunity in the durable assets (power, models) rather than a thesis-killer for AI; separate the capital cycle from the technology curve.
insights.quote: even if we have this blowup, the AI is not going away. It's not going to stop improving.

insights.claim: Google's decision to issue equity to fund AI is surprising and symbolic because Google generates enough cash that it should not need to, signaling management believes the AI TAM is so large that diluting a small percentage of a vastly bigger future pie is rational.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Equity issuance by a cash-rich incumbent is a signal of conviction in scale, not weakness; frames Google search as the high-margin 'See's Candies' funding a lower-margin but far larger AI 'BNSF'.
insights.quote: Because it's Google they can't raise money like why are they issuing equity right?

insights.claim: The Berkshire-into-Google-via-Nvidia flow is literally railroad profits recycled into AI, and Google itself is following the Berkshire playbook of moving from percentage margins (search) to absolute dollars (AI), where a lower-margin business can throw off vastly larger absolute profit.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Judge AI investments on absolute profit pools and reinvestment runway, not gross margin; high-margin businesses hit a reinvestment ceiling that low-margin, high-volume ones do not.
insights.quote: Google search was seized candies and I it feels like that's what's happening

insights.claim: Capex on AI is projected at roughly $800 billion this year and about $1.3 trillion next year, with installed compute being consumed almost immediately upon coming online.
insights.speaker: Patrick O'Shaughnessy
insights.so_what: Immediate absorption of new capacity supports the scarcity narrative now, but the risk is that payback periods measured during scarcity won't hold in eventual abundance.
insights.quote: this year it's going to be 800 billion or something that we're going to spend in capex. Next year it's supposed to be 1.3 trillion

insights.claim: Today's AI capex does not translate into usable compute for years because fab lead times exceed data-center lead times, so today's spending manifests as compute only in 2028-2029 while the shortage worsens near-term due to TSMC slowing its growth rate in 2023-2025.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: The compute shortage is structurally locked in for the next few years regardless of current spend; capacity relief is a 2028+ story.
insights.quote: No, it all manifests in compute in 2028 and 2029.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler claims that they only buy GPUs on confirmed demand and merely build empty shells is largely spin, because a built shell represents sunk fixed cost that economic logic forces them to fill rather than leave idle.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Discount management reassurances about disciplined, demand-gated buildout; sunk-cost dynamics mean overbuild risk is higher than the earnings-call narrative implies.
insights.quote: That is a great story to tell. I'm not sure how much that I think is a lot of BS because the reality is is if you've built the shell that money is sitting there.

themes.theme: US-China, TSMC Dependency and AI Geopolitics

insights.claim: A world where the US achieves decisive AI-driven military superiority would be dangerous rather than desirable, because the game-theory-optimal Chinese response would be to blow up TSMC, and US dependence on Chinese manufacturing (fabs, actuators, precursors) cannot be unwound outside of a conflict.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Challenges the bullish 'US wins AI' geopolitical narrative; the choke-point risk on TSMC and Chinese supply chains is under-priced and structural.
insights.quote: what is the game theory optimal response of China to blow up TSMC?

insights.claim: Reshoring supply chains from China is uneconomic because any competitor still sourcing from China holds such a cost advantage that firms only reshore when they have literally no choice, and even Apple's India shift is diversification, not a true exit from China.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Reshoring/insurance narratives will underdeliver absent a forcing event; cost gradients keep supply chains in China, so 'de-risking from Taiwan/China' is largely magical thinking.
insights.quote: it's like paying an insurance policy that if you don't have to pay it and it's astronomically expensive, you're just not going to pay it

insights.claim: The current AI equilibrium is favorable to the US, with OpenAI and Anthropic on the frontier, Google/Grok/Meta chasing, and Chinese labs distilling to stay roughly 6-9 months behind, and that last 6-9 months to the leading edge is the hardest gap to close.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: The China-catch-up fear may be overstated near-term; how well Meta and Grok close their own gap is the instructive test of whether the frontier is catchable at all.
insights.quote: definitely distilling these models to sort of stay about 6 to9 months behind

insights.claim: Restricting AI model releases in response to safety scares would backfire, leaving outsiders unable to observe where the true frontier is and creating a false sense of security as the gap between released models and internal frontier models widens over time.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Less open releases means the public frontier proxy becomes unreliable; investors lose signal on true capability and should expect widening released-vs-internal divergence.
insights.quote: we just stop releasing stuff and we on the outside start to lose any sense of like where exactly what is actually the frontier

themes.theme: AI Capability: Verifiable vs Unverifiable Domains

insights.claim: There is no compelling evidence that AI's proven strength in verifiable domains (coding, math) cleanly transfers to unverifiable domains or those with very long verification loops, and citing solved chess/Go is a weak counter because those were bounded, knowable domains solved by scale.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Underwrites a bar for AI generalization claims; be skeptical of TAM projections that assume verifiable-domain wins extend to open-ended knowledge work.
insights.quote: what is the evidence or where is the compelling evidence of being very good at verifiable domains cleanly translates to being very good at sort of unverifiable domains

insights.claim: Even if models never improved beyond their current state, the economic opportunity is massive because a huge share of economic activity is done by people operating like 'sentient AIs' in verifiable domains where today's models already perform.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: The monetization case does not depend on AGI; current-capability deployment into rote verifiable work is a large addressable market on its own.
insights.quote: if the models did not improve at all from where they are right now, the economic opportunity is actually massive

insights.claim: AI distilled only the end-state of human thought (published text) rather than the reasoning traces, emotion, and process behind it, so capturing those traces (e.g., via a neural-link-style interface) could be the payoff that dramatically expands model capability.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Frames a speculative next data frontier: the value is in reasoning traces, not more end-state text; watch data-provenance and interface plays that capture process.
insights.quote: It distilled all of the end state of human thought, the actual typing it on on Reddit. It doesn't have the traces

insights.claim: Medicine is simultaneously one of the largest AI opportunities and one of the most challenging, because turning machine learning onto all medical records could yield rapid discoveries, but regulation and access will heavily gate the timing.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: The AI-in-medicine thesis is real but the binding variable is regulatory/access timing, not model capability; size the opportunity but discount for red tape.
insights.quote: if you could turn an AI turn machine learning onto all the medical records, the number of discoveries and improved treatments we could come up with in a very rapid amount of time would be unbelievable

themes.theme: Aggregation Theory, Commodities and Marginal Cost

insights.claim: Aggregation theory rests on zero marginal cost and the insight that in a world of abundance the scarce, valuable problem is discovery, not distribution, so whoever solves discovery in a domain earns a virtuous feedback loop and dominates.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Apply the discovery-vs-distribution lens to AI incumbents; the durable moat is controlling demand/discovery, and zero-transaction-cost monetization at global scale.
insights.quote: in a world of abundance, the hard problem is not distribution, it's discovery

insights.claim: AI breaks the zero-marginal-cost assumption of aggregation theory because inference costs are real and, crucially, vary enormously by user, so the cost to serve a free-ChatGPT recipe-maker versus a test-time-scaling power user are not remotely in the same universe.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Blended unit economics mislead; model AI businesses by user-segment cost-to-serve, since a tail of heavy users can be structurally unprofitable at flat pricing.
insights.quote: the marginal cost question for the different user, the user using free chat GPT and the user trying to solve a a math theorem. They're not even remotely in the same universe

insights.claim: Calling open-source models 'free' is a category error: you avoid the R&D cost but still pay real inference, and models like Kimi or GLM are expensive to serve, with a significantly higher cost per answer.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Open-weight does not mean cheap at scale; cost-to-serve, not licensing, determines competitiveness, and structurally lower serving cost is a real moat.
insights.quote: Kimmy is very expensive to serve. The cost per answer is significantly higher.

insights.claim: Both intelligence and compute may end up as commodities, and commodities change the world precisely because they are available to everyone, whereas differentiated high-margin products carry lower TAMs due to elasticity constraints on willingness to pay.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Commoditization of intelligence favors free/ad-supported scale players over premium differentiated pricing; TAM expands as price approaches marginal cost.
insights.quote: differentiated products by definition have lower TAMs because you're like not there's a elasticity aspect to it

insights.claim: In commodity markets price is set by the marginal supplier and cost-to-serve is all that matters, so operators run assets (ships, fabs, memory lines) at any price above marginal cost because depreciation is an accounting figment on money already spent.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: If AI compute commoditizes, expect price wars to marginal cost with paper losses but continued operation; apply commodity cyclicality, not software economics, to data centers.
insights.quote: But in a commodity market, the price is set by the marginal supplier.

themes.theme: Consumer vs Enterprise Business Models and Advertising

insights.claim: Silicon Valley must relearn every decade that consumers will not pay for software and do not care about being productive, so consumer AI is naturally an advertising business, while enterprises pay because they can convert productivity into return on their employees.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Consumer AI monetization converges on advertising; subscription-only consumer AI (the Dropbox trap) will undermonetize versus an ad flywheel.
insights.quote: consumers do not want to pay for software. And number two, consumers do not care about being productive

insights.claim: OpenAI replayed the Dropbox story at ~100x scale by selling consumer subscriptions and selling a lot but not enough, and its late pivot to advertising is a costly mistake because an early ad flywheel would have made it a killer ad product and put Google and Meta in far bigger trouble.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: OpenAI's ad rollout (retailer connections, purchase tracking) is worth watching, but the delayed start ceded a strategic advantage against the incumbent ad platforms.
insights.quote: There's a bit where had they leaned into advertising immediately as soon as Chat GPT was a hit, I think they would have a killer ad product right now.

insights.claim: Advertising-funded consumer businesses have near-zero price elasticity because advertisers, not consumers, bear price increases, so monetization per consumer can rise without the churn risk that constrains subscription models like Netflix.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Ad-model platforms have more durable pricing power than subscription models; the ability to raise monetization without consumer rebellion is a structural advantage.
insights.quote: the thing about advertising with consumers is your ability to monetize the consumer goes up in because the advertisers bearing the price increase. So there's zero elasticity issues

insights.claim: Microsoft's shift toward usage-based AI pricing on top of its ~$100/user E7 plan is a fraught, potentially model-breaking move because it untethers revenue from headcount and forces customers to re-evaluate monthly what they are paying for and how good each product is.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Usage-based AI billing threatens Microsoft's thoughtless per-seat revenue stream by inviting product-by-product scrutiny; watch for churn/unbundling risk as customers start counting tokens.
insights.quote: The moment you start having to think about how much you're paying, it's not just that that's a new decision.

insights.claim: Google and Meta capture the largest current AI monetization gains, and models give ad platforms a unique advantage because ad performance is itself a verifiable domain, letting them validate AI-generated creative against a global A/B-test marketplace of human clicks and purchases.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Ad incumbents own a proprietary verification/feedback loop for generative content; a few-percentage-point lift in ad relevance from LLM prediction is worth billions and justifies their frontier spend.
insights.quote: How do you verify if a generated image is good for an ad? Does the ad sell or not?

themes.theme: Commodity Cycles: Memory, Fabs and Overbuild Risk

insights.claim: Memory is prone to violent boom-bust cycles where shortages spur over-investment and price plunges wash out marginal producers, and Samsung historically took over the market by investing counter-cyclically into downturns, wiping out Japanese makers.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Counter-cyclical capex discipline is the winning strategy in commodity semis; apply the same overbuild-and-washout template to AI data-center capacity.
insights.quote: the way to take over the market is to invest into downturns so that you're ready when the next cycle comes around

insights.claim: By restricting memory supply during the AI shortage, the three-maker memory oligopoly is painting a target on its back, spurring algorithmic efforts to use less memory, Apple lobbying for Chinese memory, and long-run substitution that could hurt them like Iran's Strait of Hormuz leverage.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Exercising commodity pricing power invites permanent workarounds; today's memory pricing strength may sow the seeds of long-run demand destruction and new entrants.
insights.quote: The issue with the straight of moose is it's very effective. It's more effective if you don't use it

insights.claim: TSMC has offloaded overcapacity risk onto Big Tech customers, whose foregone revenue from insufficient compute is the manifestation of that risk, and TSMC's conservatism echoes prior cycles because it expects each fab to run 30 years.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Risk never disappears, it relocates; TSMC's restraint means the compute shortage is a transfer of risk to hyperscalers, showing up as foregone profit rather than losses.
insights.quote: Risk doesn't disappear. It just moves.

insights.claim: The acute AI compute shortage is what ultimately saves Intel and Samsung's foundry ambitions, because Big Tech's foregone revenue makes it worth enduring the pain of qualifying second sources, and a major first customer announcement for Intel is likely near.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Scarcity, not policy, is the catalyst for Intel/Samsung foundry viability; a headline anchor-customer partnership for Intel foundry is a watch item.
insights.quote: The scarcity is what ultimately saved Intel.

insights.claim: No customer will pay for geopolitical or second-source insurance when its expected value is negative, so the only way to diversify away from TSMC is a compute use case so massive that firms are economically incentivized to bring Intel/Samsung up to speed, yielding the geopolitical hedge for free.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Supply-chain resilience gets funded only as a byproduct of profit incentives, not as standalone insurance; the AI demand surge is the mechanism that finally diversifies fab dependency.
insights.quote: no one's going to pay insurance they don't need to pay when that insurance expected value is is negative

themes.theme: Big Tech Setups: Amazon, Apple, Microsoft, Meta

insights.claim: Amazon has the most interesting setup because it is its own first-best customer, scaling internal needs (AWS, logistics, Graviton, Trainium, AI call-center software) into external products, giving it the deepest moat and organic ability to spawn new business lines.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Amazon's first-best-customer flywheel (hiding early crappy silicon inside managed services to build volume) makes its core impervious to model-level AI disruption; a durable compounder.
insights.quote: they build for them. They are their first best customer

insights.claim: Apple is well-positioned to sit out frontier AI because as an aggregator owning customer access it can source AI models from suppliers as needed, run inference on-device using the customer's own electricity, and its deterministic hardware DNA is ill-suited to probabilistic AI anyway.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Apple not building frontier AI is defensible, not a fatal miss; the risk is an ambient/cloud AI paradigm shifting the center of gravity off the phone, a Microsoft-missed-mobile-style trap.
insights.quote: Apple is the king of deterministic products

insights.claim: Microsoft's off-frontier strategy is the rational IBM-in-the-1990s middleware play, positioning itself as the stable, backwards-compatible platform that helps enterprises adopt AI without handing crown jewels to the labs, trading best-in-class experience for dependability.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Microsoft's data-center spend skews to inference not training, making its demand-driven buildout more believable; but the strategy is simultaneously sound and existentially desperate.
insights.quote: It's the IBM play of the '9s.

insights.claim: Microsoft's software franchise faces a real long-run threat because AI is surprisingly good at the tedious, repetitive work of migrating systems of record, and its true value is the user interface layer that agentic tools like Codex and Claude aim directly at.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: The lock-in of systems of record weakens when AI can cheaply migrate them; Microsoft's UI/interaction layer is the contested surface, making its position both sound and desperate.
insights.quote: one reason why systems of records are so powerful is it's so hard to move them to somewhere else... Oh AI is actually surprisingly good at that

insights.claim: Meta pays literally nothing for the user-generated content that monetizes Instagram, so AI-generated content is margin-dilutive for Meta (worse than free) even as it could be positive for YouTube, whose revenue-share model means inference-generated content could cost less than creator payouts.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: AI content economics cut opposite ways across platforms: accretive for revenue-share YouTube, dilutive for zero-cost-content Meta; model each platform's content cost structure before assuming AI content is a win.
insights.quote: For meta AI generated content to the extent they're the ones generating it is actually a worse margin profile than what they have today. What they have today is free.

insights.claim: TikTok took share from Meta because Meta miscategorized it as a social network when it is actually an entertainment product that surfaces the best content from the entire network rather than your follow graph, forcing Meta to convert Instagram/Reels into a non-social entertainment feed.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: The social-graph constraint is an artificial limit on content quality; in an AI world, genuine human social connection could become valuable and differentiated again, a potential Meta tailwind.
insights.quote: Tik Tok is classified as a social network and it's not a social network at all. Tik Tok is an entertainment product.

insights.claim: OpenAI and Anthropic are the riskiest but highest-upside frontier players because their quasi-religious belief that they are creating God, combined with the existential need to build a working business to survive, drives outsized effort in a way incumbents cannot replicate.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Belief plus survival pressure is an under-modeled competitive asset; the labs' incentive structure gives them an edge over incumbents where 'search just needs to not die too quickly.'
insights.quote: the two religious organizations in Silicon Valley are the sort of like open kind of like mainline... that's anthropic like they're they're all in

insights.claim: Meta pursuing the frontier by hiring a wholly new team from scratch is an insane bet only explicable as pure founder energy from Mark Zuckerberg, since a Meta run by anyone else would simply double down on its amazing existing ad business.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Meta's frontier push is founder-driven, not consensus-rational; weigh it as a Zuckerberg conviction bet, and note his prior ~$100B Oculus spend as a reason markets may resist funding it.
insights.quote: Meta being like actually we're going to hire a completely new team and we're going to start from scratch. This all again is pretty insane.

insights.claim: SpaceX AI has the weakest case among frontier contenders because its differentiation is data centers in space, and if that plays out it need not own its own model, making the billions spent building one a questionable expense; the cursor acquisition, however, makes strong strategic sense.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Value the space-datacenter optionality separately from the model effort; owning a model may be redundant to the infrastructure edge, though the Cursor deal is a positive tactical signal.
insights.quote: the case for SpaceX AI is probably the weakest because the data center and space play is so highly differentiated

insights.claim: For a digital company it may be more reckless to NOT be on the AI frontier than to spend on it, because all digital businesses are ultimately threatened by AI, so staying off-frontier (Microsoft's choice) buys free cash flow at the cost of long-run existential exposure.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Reframes frontier capex as defensive necessity rather than optional moonshot for digital incumbents; the off-frontier cash cow (Microsoft's $20B quarterly FCF) is the trade-off, not a free lunch.
insights.quote: it is actually more reckless to not be on the frontier if you're a digital company

themes.theme: Nvidia, Circular Financing and the Power Endgame

insights.claim: Nvidia is not truly maintaining its margins in 2026; it is disguising price cuts through circular financing, because taking equity in neoclouds and guaranteeing to buy their compute lowers their cost of capital only because Nvidia has assumed risk, which is a negative-expected-value diminution of profitability.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Adjust Nvidia's true economics for off-balance-sheet risk assumption; headline margins overstate profitability once vendor-financing guarantees are marked as implicit price cuts.
insights.quote: a lot of what Nvidia is doing is how can we maintain our margins even if the wide view sort of discounted cash flow expected value holistic view of our company

insights.claim: Nvidia's ultimate competitive threat is the hyperscalers, especially Google and Amazon, who are selling their own chips (Google already sold ~20% of TPU capacity to Anthropic; Amazon signaled external Trainium sales) as commodities, not on differentiation, so they don't cannibalize their clouds.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: The bear case on Nvidia is hyperscaler custom silicon plus superior cost of capital; watch external TPU/Trainium sales as evidence the commodity-chip flank is opening.
insights.quote: Google already made a deal to sell sell like 20% of their TPUs to anthropic.

insights.claim: The decisive advantage in the AI buildout is cost of capital, and hyperscalers (able to issue equity like Google) have a structurally lower cost of capital than the neoclouds buying Nvidia, which is why the Nvidia deal pairs with the Google equity issuance.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: In a capital fight, higher monetization capacity and equity access beat vendor-financed neoclouds; the winners are those who can fund compute most cheaply, not those with the best chips.
insights.quote: It's a capital fight. They have a lower cost of capital than the Neoclouds do.

insights.claim: Buyers choose Nvidia for fungibility, not superiority, because CUDA's moat is diminished as models no longer care what hardware they run on, but Nvidia remains the easiest chip to rent out, sustaining a weakened but real moat for build-and-lease players like SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Nvidia's durable edge is now liquidity/fungibility of its installed base rather than software lock-in; that supports rentable-capacity demand but is a thinner moat than CUDA once was.
insights.quote: CUDA's mode is dramatically diminished because the models don't care what they run on

insights.claim: Nvidia's best-case scenario is the world running out of power, because acute power constraints force everyone to buy the most token-efficient chips (which Nvidia still makes), and Jensen likely expected power scarcity to become Nvidia's moat sooner than it has.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Power abundance is bearish for Nvidia because it buys Amazon and Google time to make Trainium/TPU efficiency-competitive; track US power capacity additions as a leading indicator for Nvidia's moat.
insights.quote: the longer we have enough power, the more time Amazon has to make Tranium better, the more time Google has to to make TPUs competitive

insights.claim: The US has brought far more power online than expected via behind-the-meter gas (West Texas), restarted nuclear plants, and other measures, delaying the power constraint longer than anyone including Jensen Huang anticipated.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: Delayed power scarcity undercuts a key Nvidia bull thesis and buys custom-silicon competitors time; the durable AI-bubble legacy asset is power infrastructure, akin to dark fiber after dot-com.
insights.quote: I think the US has actually brought a lot more power online than expected

insights.claim: The lasting payoff of an AI bubble should be power infrastructure, analogous to how dot-com left dark fiber that Google bought cheaply and how railroad bonds sold to retail investors ultimately funded enduring GDP contribution.
insights.speaker: Ben Thompson
insights.so_what: GPUs depreciate fast and data centers are transient, so the durable investable residue of the AI cycle is energy generation capacity; position for a post-bust world of energy abundance.
insights.quote: you want a bubble that produces something that lasts... It's like power. It has to be power.
